records.name: Uruguay
records.summary:
Uruguay is one of Latin America's safest and most progressive destinations for trans visitors. The Comprehensive Law for Trans People (Law 19,684, 2018) provides legal gender recognition by administrative self-declaration (no surgery or diagnosis required), a reparation pension for trans victims of institutional violence, and a state employment quota for trans people. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013 (Latin America's first), and bathroom access is legally protected.

The country is consistently ranked among Latin America's safest (Global Peace Index), with a "strong democratic governance structure and positive record of upholding political rights and civil liberties" (Freedom House). However, a 29-year-old trans woman, Joana, was shot dead in her home in Montevideo in July 2025 (the assailant was sentenced to 7 years), and discrimination incidents have been documented at a hospital (San Carlos) and a bank (BROU). Freedom House notes "disparities in treatment" for transgender people despite legal equality.

For a visitor: no border friction, bathrooms protected, no criminalisation, and Montevideo is welcoming.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): broad protections - same-sex marriage since 2013, adoption since 2009, accessible legal gender recognition; since 2021 more than 120 trans people have accessed a reparation pension for institutional violence suffered during the 1973-1985 dictatorship; anti-discrimination law explicitly covers SOGI and hate-crime laws include SOGI aggravating circumstances.

Cornell Law School resource on Uruguay's Ley N° 19684 (2018), the Comprehensive Law for Trans People: ensures the right to a life free of discrimination and stigmatisation; the right to free development of personality per one's gender identity regardless of biological/genetic/anatomical factors; right to identification matching gender identity; includes reparation mechanisms.

Equaldex data for Montevideo (governed by federal Uruguay law): homosexuality legal, marriage legal, gender change with no restrictions, gender-affirming care legal, full ban on intersex infant surgery, hate-crime protections cover SOGI, discrimination illegal, conversion therapy banned, bathroom access protected.

Uruguayan Presidency (Nov 2018, in Spanish): the Executive promulgated the Comprehensive Law for Trans Persons (Law 19,684) - the right to gender identity and a life free of discrimination, name/sex change on identity documents, and a reparation regime for trans people born before 31 December 1975 who suffered institutional violence or deprivation of liberty.

Freedom House 2024 for Uruguay: 'Free' (96/100) - historically strong democratic governance; disparities remain in treatment and political representation of women, transgender people, Afro-Uruguayans and the Indigenous population.

Trans Lives Matter / TDoR memorial entry (July 2025): Joana, 29, a trans woman shot in the head at her home in Montevideo's Bella Italia neighbourhood; police hypothesised the attack targeted the man with her and she was a collateral victim; the perpetrator was sentenced to 7 years; the state expressed sorrow.

la diaria (May 2024, in Spanish): a trans user denounced mistreatment and discrimination at the San Carlos hospital - Andrea Gianneo, previously brutally beaten by a driver in Piriápolis (prompting a Piria Pride mobilisation), discussed the case with the health-centre director alongside a criminal complaint.

Montevideo Portal (Sept 2025, in Spanish): a trans woman in a discrimination lawsuit against state bank BROU denounces concealment of evidence - Beccah Rivas says the bank did not deliver the main record requested by the prosecutor and that she lost her job after publicising the case.

PinkNews (Dec 2007): Uruguay became the first Latin American country to recognise same-sex civil unions - President Tabare Vazquez signed the law granting cohabiting couples (5+ years) the same rights as married couples, 'of any sex, identity, orientation or sexual option'; the Episcopal Conference of Uruguay attacked the validity of gay relationships.

records.name: United States
records.summary:
The United States demands real caution from trans visitors — and uniquely among Western nations, is the subject of official trans-traveler warnings from at least eight European allied governments (Germany, Finland, Denmark, and others, March 2025) following executive orders requiring federal documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. A German traveler, Jessica Brösche, was detained at the US border for weeks and deported (January 2025); a CBP officer faces a lawsuit for alleged sexual contact with a trans traveler at Boston Logan Airport. Trans Americans have been stranded with mismatched passports.

Enforcement extends into daily life: in April 2025 a trans woman was arrested and jailed overnight under Florida's bathroom law — believed to be the first such arrest — and a trans man was detained by police in South Carolina for using a women's restroom. State-level bathroom laws, misgendering statutes, and a hostile federal posture coexist with strong protections in blue states and cities.

sources.claim: Advocates for Trans Equality 'Know Your Rights' guide to US airport security (TSA): body-scanner flags, pat-downs, documentation mismatches, and how to request alternative screening.

Human Rights Watch (Mar 2026): 'US State Revokes Gender-Affirming Identification' — across Kansas, trans people receive letters voiding their driver's licenses under a law invalidating birth certificates and IDs that do not match sex assigned at birth and barring bathroom use inconsistent with it.

AP (Feb 2026): 'New law puts Kansas at vanguard of denying trans identities on drivers licenses, birth certificates' — Kansas prevents transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and licenses; rights groups call it a template for other states.

Movement Advancement Project equality map: bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity - 9 states + 1 territory ban such use in all government-owned buildings and spaces including K-12 schools, colleges and more; some bans extend to airports, public parks and other government spaces.

USA Today (March 2025): how the new State Department rule blocks trans travellers - Trump's executive order requires all government identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; passports are issued only with markers matching 'biological sex'; first-person account of a trans man flagged at airport security and accused of using a fake ID due to a licence/passport mismatch.

AP (Apr 2025): 'Transgender student's arrest for violating Florida bathroom law is thought to be a first' — a trans student declared 'I am here to break the law' and was handcuffed in a women's restroom at the state capitol; civil-rights attorneys say it is the first known arrest under the state's bathroom-restriction law.

Lambda Legal FAQ on passport and identity-document information for the transgender community (updated March 2026): what the January 2025 'Gender Order' means for passports, REAL IDs and other documents; the restrictive passport policy is in effect (as of Nov 2025); practical guidance for travellers, noting it is informational, not legal advice.

Erin In The Morning anti-trans national legal risk assessment map (July 2026): Idaho becomes the fourth 'Do Not Travel' state for transgender people - bathroom usage can lead to 5-year prison sentences; South Carolina expanded its bathroom ban to universities; state-by-state risk grading for trans people.

Human Rights Campaign resource on travel and passport rights for transgender people: what the January 2025 executive order ('sex at conception' on all government ID) did - the State Department immediately stopped allowing trans, nonbinary and intersex people to update sex designations.

CNN (Apr 2025): 'Countries issue advisories about trans people traveling to the United States' — multiple foreign governments warn their trans citizens about travelling to the US over identity-document and data rules.

Axios (March 2025): Trump's transgender rights rollbacks prompt allies to adjust travel warnings - at least eight European countries (including Finland and Denmark) adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the US; advisories follow detentions of European citizens over visa issues.
Vox (March 2026): the fight over transgender rights in America has entered a new phase - the policy fight is moving well beyond sports and youth medicine into broader areas.

Movement Advancement Project equality map on identity-document laws and policies: state-by-state driver's license gender-marker change processes and options (22 states + D.C. allow M, F or X); accurate markers reduce risk of violence and discrimination.

Queer Compass travel-safety guide (April 2026): is the US safe for LGBTQ+ travellers in 2026? - same-sex activity legal, but protections vary heavily by state; trans, non-binary and intersex travellers face extra uncertainty around passports, visas, gender markers, facilities and healthcare; border/visa processes can involve social-media and device checks; credible reporting of travellers cancelling trips or facing extra scrutiny.

Condé Nast Traveler (Feb 2025): what to know about the new policy on passport gender markers - the State Department stopped processing X-marker passports and markers not matching sex assigned at birth; existing X-marker passports remain valid until expiration; new applications processed only as M or F per supporting documents.

records.name: Uzbekistan
records.summary:
Uzbekistan is dangerous for trans visitors. Article 120 of the Criminal Code criminalises male same-sex conduct (up to 3 years) — and Human Dignity Trust notes transgender people may be targeted under it, since there is no legal gender recognition and trans people are legally their birth sex. There is substantial evidence of recent enforcement: frequent arrests, and extortion by threat of arrest, with police as the most common perpetrators of anti-LGBT violence; torture goes unpunished (HRW). Because of criminalisation, victims cannot report violence to authorities.

ECOM's 2024 national report documents continuing rights violations, and the Justice Ministry denies registration to independent human-rights groups — no community infrastructure can operate openly. There is no documented trans-visitor case, but the legal mechanism (birth-sex status + Art 120) means a trans visitor discovered in a same-sex-appearing relationship faces direct prosecution risk, and discovery itself invites extortion.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Uzbekistan's criminalisation of same-sex activity (Article 120 of the criminal code, up to 3 years).

HRW World Report 2024 Uzbekistan chapter: includes a Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity section amid a deteriorating human-rights record (harassment of bloggers, Karakalpakstan impunity, constitutional changes).

ECOM national report (2024) on violations of the rights of LGBT people in Uzbekistan: legislation, anti-discrimination legislation, criminalisation of HIV transmission, legal gender recognition, access to human rights, right to health and right to work.
UK Home Office CPIN Uzbekistan: sexual orientation and gender identity or expression (July 2024): official country-of-origin information and assessment for asylum claims.
US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Uzbekistan: official assessment - same-sex conduct criminalised under Article 120; police abuse and societal stigma; no legal protections.
US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Uzbekistan: official assessment - continued criminalisation under Article 120, societal discrimination, and no anti-discrimination protections.
HRW (March 2021): 'Uzbekistan: Gay Men Face Abuse in Prison' - documents the abuse, extortion and violence gay men face in prison under Article 120 prosecutions.

records.name: Vatican City
records.summary:
Vatican City is workable for trans visitors — and an unusual case: it is a 0.49 km² tourist enclave (museums, basilica, square) with essentially no resident jurisdiction a traveler can fall afoul of. Nothing about being trans is criminalised; there are no bathrooms inspections, no morality police, and the Swiss Guards and gendarmerie do not police tourist gender expression. Millions of tourists of every presentation visit annually without incident; entry is via Rome with no border formality.

The doctrinal climate is hostile: the 2024 declaration "Infinite Dignity" condemned gender-affirming surgery and "gender theory" as violations of human dignity, and there is obviously no legal recognition or protection of any kind. But this is a climate signal, not a traveler-facing mechanism — the realistic worst case for a visitor is being refused entry to the basilica over a dress-code dispute (shoulders/knees rules apply to everyone). Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.

sources.claim: PinkNews (Oct 2008): the Vatican blocked the appointment of a gay French diplomat (Jean-Loup Kuhn-Delforge, in a civil pact) as envoy to the Holy See, also rejecting a divorced candidate - 'The Roman Catholic Church is opposed to gay rights and any attempts to protect or recognise gay relationships in law.'

Vatican Congregation for Catholic Education (2019): 'Male and Female He Created Them - Towards a Path of Dialogue on the Question of Gender Theory in Education' - the Vatican's educational document opposing 'gender theory', which it says 'denies the difference and reciprocity in nature of a man and a woman' and 'eliminat[es] the anthropological basis of the family'.

records.name: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines
records.summary: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines demands real caution — the Eastern Caribbean outlier: its High Court UPHELD the buggery laws in 2024 (unlike its neighbours), so criminalisation (10 years) remains formally in force. Enforcement is rare, but the legal floor and judicial hostility distinguish it from the decriminalised neighbours.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust page documents Eastern Caribbean constitutional challenges; Saint Vincent and the Grenadines retains colonial-era buggery and gross-indecency laws.
NOTE: This HRW article is about Antigua and Barbuda's 2022 ruling, not Saint Vincent and the Grenadines specifically; included as Eastern Caribbean regional context.

GlobalGayz 'Gay Life in St Vincent and The Grenadines' (Sept 2012): 'A Bad Situation and a Bad Law' - homosexuality is illegal, stigmatised and not tolerated; St Vincent has no LGBT organisation (unlike Grenada); most LGBT people marry opposite-gender spouses or live on the 'down-low'; the Caribbean HIV/AIDS Alliance bridges the gap indirectly.

PinkNews (Feb 2024): Saint Vincent and the Grenadines' High Court upheld the ban on gay sex - sections 146 (up to 10 years for anal intercourse) and 148 (5 years for 'gross indecency') of the Criminal Code 1988 remain; the challenge by Kevin Vinc Johnson and Sean Macleish, who said they were forced to leave the country, was rejected; Justice Esco Henry found the laws 'reasonably required'.
HRW (July 2023): 'Saint Vincent and the Grenadines: LGBT People Face Bias' - documents discrimination and violence against LGBT Vincentians ahead of the court ruling.

ECADE press release (Feb 2024): 'High Court ruling undermines the rights of LGBTQ+ Vincentians' - the dismissal of the challenge to sections 146 and 148 'weaponised hate... sanctioned by the highest court' (VincyCHAP); the Attorney General was joined by religious groups as interested parties; the ruling legitimises violence and abuses.

records.name: Venezuela
records.summary:
Venezuela demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing about gender expression is criminalised, but Venezuela has achieved no meaningful legal recognition for LGBTIQ+ people: no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, no hate-crime statute. Since the disputed July 2024 election, activists document unprecedented persecution of the LGBTQ community amid the broader repression wave, and arbitrary detention powers are used broadly against perceived dissidents.

Caracas has a small visible scene, and trans women have historically been a visible part of urban life, but the economic collapse means healthcare (including HRT access) is severely degraded, police are predatory toward everyone, and there is no institutional recourse. The risk profile for a visitor is less about trans-specific targeting and more about the combination of zero legal protection, arbitrary state power, and high general violence.

sources.claim: Washington Blade (Sep 2024): 'LGBTQ Venezuelans face unprecedented persecution after disputed election' — post-election crackdowns ensnare LGBTQ people; detention and abuse reported.
EUAA Venezuela Country Focus, section 3.5 'LGBTIQ+ persons': country-of-origin assessment of the situation of LGBTIQ+ persons in Venezuela.
NOTE: The AFS/Vance Center LGBTQ guide on Venezuela (Oct 2024) returned no extractable text at fetch time (image-based PDF).

SMH/Reuters (Aug 2015): Venezuela's first transgender candidate, Tamara Adrian, registered for Congress under her given male name (Thomas) because Venezuelan law does not allow legal gender change despite her 2002 surgery; she argued Venezuela, with Paraguay, Guyana, Suriname and Peru, has done little for equal rights.

Crónica Uno (March 2023, in Spanish): an Equilibrium Cende survey found 76% of Venezuelans support LGBTIQ people being honest about their sexual orientation and gender identity - majority public support for equal rights.

Sabina Becker blog (Jan 2014): 'Equal marriage: coming soon to Venezuela?' - the sex/gender diversity community presented the egalitarian civil-marriage bill to modify Article 44 of the Civil Code; recalls the TSJ's 2008 Sentence 190 that the constitution does not discriminate on sexual orientation.

El Mundo (Dec 2015, in Spanish): Amnesty International declared Rosmit Mantilla - deputy-elect and openly gay activist of Voluntad Popular, founder of Proinclusión which first requested same-sex marriage in the National Assembly - a prisoner of conscience, held in Sebin; he became the first openly gay parliamentarian in Venezuela's history.

records.name: British Virgin Islands
records.summary:
Same-sex intimacy in the British Virgin Islands was decriminalised in January 2001 by order of the administering state's Privy Council, after the local legislature refused to act — a local legislator's 'there is nothing we can do about it' captured the resentment with which the reform landed. Family status remains contested rather than settled: in 2022 the Court of Appeal refused the local churches council's attempt to appeal a judgment in favour of two women, married in the UK, who were seeking recognition of their marriage and a declaration that the prohibition is unconstitutional — the court finding the proposed appeal had no realistic prospect of success.

Visitors encounter a tolerant-but-quiet society: travel surveys rate these twin islands among the more gay-welcoming in the Caribbean while noting resistance beneath the surface, with most local hostility 'silent and invisible' and most visitors hardly noticing either way. Discretion, not danger, is the operative norm.

sources.claim: BBC News (Feb 2014): 'Gay rights map: Notes on the data' - the BBC/UN OHCHR gay-rights map and timeline methodology built on ILGA data (context for the British Virgin Islands as a UK territory).

AP (Jan 2001): Britain scrapped homosexuality laws in its five Caribbean territories (including the British Virgin Islands) via Privy Council order after local legislatures refused; BVI legislator Orlando Smith: 'There is nothing we can do about it.'

GlobalGayz 'Gay Life in British Virgin Islands' (Aug 2012/2017): the BVI and USVI are 'among the more gay welcoming islands in the Caribbean, but are not without resistance and secret lives'; most native homophobia is 'silent and invisible' and most tourists hardly notice.

BVI News (July 2022): the BVI Christian Council lost its proposed appeal in the case of Kinisha Forbes and Kirsten Lettsome - a couple married in the UK seeking recognition of their marriage under BVI law and a ruling that the same-sex marriage prohibition is unconstitutional; Judge Jack ruled the appeal had 'no realistic prospect of success'.

records.name: U.S. Virgin Islands
records.summary:
A small US territory: federal document and airport policy applies, and the 2025–26 federal turn is felt through it (marker disputes, screening friction) with no local statute to soften it. Locally the record is quietly protective rather than hostile: the Attorney General ruled in 2017 that the human-rights law's sex provision covers transgender students — an official extension of territorial protection — and local media framed the community's position after the 2016 federal shock as 'losses... but reason for hope.'

No criminalisation, documented anti-trans enforcement or care ban appears in the audited record; equally, protection rests on an attorney-general's interpretation rather than legislation, and the islands' scale (tens of thousands across three main islands) means high everyday recognition risk. Federal rollback above, a thin but genuinely welcoming local posture beneath.

sources.claim: Advocates for Trans Equality 'Know Your Rights' guide to US airport security (TSA): body-scanner flags, pat-downs, documentation mismatches, and how to request alternative screening - relevant to the US Virgin Islands as a US territory under TSA procedures.

Human Rights Watch (Mar 2026): 'US State Revokes Gender-Affirming Identification' — Kansas voids birth certificates and driver's licenses not matching sex assigned at birth; US document-policy context relevant to US territories.
St. John Source (March 2017): the Attorney General ruled the USVI anti-discrimination law applies to transgender students - official interpretation extending territorial protections.
St. Thomas Source (July 2017): 'LGBTQ community see losses in territory but reason for hope' - local reporting on the community's setbacks and prospects in the USVI.
